concepts.name: National Emergency (Article 352): grounds, proclamation and judicial review
concepts.description: Part XVIII, the three kinds of emergency, the grounds of a National Emergency, who must recommend it, the changes made by the 38th, 42nd and 44th Amendments and judicial review.
concepts.idea: A National Emergency may be proclaimed only on war, external aggression or armed rebellion (or imminent danger of them), on the written recommendation of the Cabinet, and the proclamation is open to judicial review.
concepts.rule: The Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360) and make the federal system work as a unitary one without a formal amendment. The Constitution stipulates three emergencies: Article 352 (war, external aggression or armed rebellion; the Constitution calls it 'proclamation of emergency'), Article 356 (failure of constitutional machinery in states) and Article 360 (financial). The President can proclaim a National Emergency even before the event if satisfied that there is imminent danger; the 38th Amendment (1975) allowed different proclamations on different grounds, the 42nd (1976) allowed limiting it to a part of India, and the 44th (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' by 'armed rebellion' and required the written recommendation of the Cabinet. The 38th Amendment's immunity from judicial review was deleted by the 44th, and Minerva Mills (1980) held that a proclamation can be challenged for malafide, wholly extraneous or irrelevant facts, or absurdity or perversity (pp.259-260).
concepts.example: In June 1975 the Prime Minister advised the President without consulting the Cabinet, which was informed afterwards; the 44th Amendment's written-recommendation rule closed this route.

concepts.name: National Emergency: parliamentary approval, duration and revocation
concepts.description: Time limit and majority for approval, effect of dissolution of the Lok Sabha, six-monthly continuance, revocation by the President and by the Lok Sabha, and the 44th Amendment changes.
concepts.idea: A National Emergency lapses unless both Houses approve it by a special majority within one month, continues only with approval every six months, and the Lok Sabha can force its revocation by a simple majority.
concepts.rule: The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within one month (originally two months; reduced by the 44th Amendment). If the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the proclamation survives until 30 days from the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha, provided the Rajya Sabha has meanwhile approved it. Once approved it continues for six months and can be extended indefinitely with approval every six months (added by the 44th Amendment; earlier it could last as long as the Cabinet desired). Every approving resolution needs a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). The President may revoke it any time by a subsequent proclamation without approval, and must revoke it if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution of disapproval, for which a special sitting must be held within 14 days on the written notice of one-tenth of its members (pp.260-261).
concepts.example: A proclamation issued while the Lok Sabha stands dissolved survives only if the Rajya Sabha approves it in the meantime, and then until 30 days after the reconstituted Lok Sabha first sits.

concepts.name: National Emergency: effect on Centre-state relations and on the life of legislatures
concepts.description: Executive, legislative and financial consequences for the states, the ordinance power, the 42nd Amendment extension, and extension of the term of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.
concepts.idea: A National Emergency turns the federal system unitary: the Centre directs the states on any matter, Parliament legislates on the State List, revenues can be modified, and legislatures' terms can be extended, while state governments and legislatures are not suspended.
concepts.rule: Effects are grouped as Centre-state relations (executive, legislative, financial), the life of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, and Fundamental Rights. The Centre can direct any state on any matter, but state governments are not suspended. Parliament can legislate on the State List, the state legislature is not suspended but is subject to Parliament's overriding power, such laws become inoperative six months after the Emergency ceases, and the President can issue ordinances on state subjects when Parliament is not in session. The 42nd Amendment extended the executive and legislative consequences to any other state. The President can reduce or cancel financial transfers to the states till the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ceases, and the order is laid before both Houses. The life of the Lok Sabha or an assembly can be extended by law one year at a time, not beyond six months after the Emergency ceases (pp.261-262).
concepts.example: The term of the Fifth Lok Sabha (1971-77) was extended twice, one year each time, during the 1975 Emergency.

concepts.name: National Emergency and the Fundamental Rights: Articles 358 and 359
concepts.description: Automatic suspension of Article 19 under Article 358, suspension of enforcement under Article 359, the 44th Amendment limits, and the seven-point distinction between the two Articles.
concepts.idea: Article 358 automatically suspends the Article 19 freedoms (only in an External Emergency), while Article 359 lets the President suspend only the enforcement of specified rights, never of Articles 20 and 21.
concepts.rule: Articles 358 and 359 describe the effect of a National Emergency on the Fundamental Rights. Under Article 358 the six rights of Article 19 are automatically suspended on proclamation, no separate order is needed, the State may make any law or take any executive action abridging them, and Article 19 revives when the Emergency ceases, though no remedy lies for what was done. Article 359 authorises the President to suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights; the rights are not suspended, only their enforcement, only for those named in the Presidential Order, for the Emergency or a shorter period, for the whole or part of the country. The 44th Amendment confined Article 358 to an Emergency on war or external aggression, barred suspension of the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21, and limited the protection to laws related to the Emergency and executive action taken under them. Article 359 operates in both External and Internal Emergencies (pp.262-264).
concepts.example: A law curbing freedom of speech made during an Emergency declared on armed rebellion is not automatically protected by Article 358.

concepts.name: President's Rule (Article 356): grounds, approval, duration and consequences
concepts.description: Articles 355, 356 and 365, parliamentary approval and duration, the 44th Amendment limit beyond one year, the powers of the President, laws for the state, the High Court and the comparison with a National Emergency.
concepts.idea: President's Rule follows failure of the constitutional machinery in a state, needs approval of Parliament by simple majority within two months, lasts up to three years, and transfers the state's executive and legislative powers to the Centre.
concepts.rule: Article 355 imposes a duty on the Centre to protect every state and ensure its government is carried on according to the Constitution; Article 356 is invoked on the Governor's report or otherwise, and Article 365 permits the President to hold that machinery has failed if a state does not comply with a Centre's direction. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months by a simple majority, continues for six months and can be extended with approval every six months up to three years. Beyond one year, extension needs a National Emergency in operation and an Election Commission certificate that elections cannot be held (44th Amendment). The President takes over the state government's functions, may declare that Parliament will exercise the legislature's powers, the council of ministers is dismissed, the assembly is suspended or dissolved, Parliament may delegate law-making to the President, and the High Court is untouched. Laws so made continue after the Rule unless repealed, altered or re-enacted by the state legislature (pp.265-267).
concepts.example: A state assembly is suspended; the Governor, on behalf of the President, runs the state with the chief secretary, and Parliament passes the state budget.

concepts.name: Use and misuse of Article 356: judicial review, the Bommai case and proper and improper use
concepts.description: Arbitrary imposition of President's Rule (1977, 1980, 1992), Ambedkar and Kamath on Article 356, the 38th and 44th Amendments on judicial review, the ten Bommai propositions and the Sarkaria-based lists of proper and improper use.
concepts.idea: Article 356 was widely misused for political ends until the Bommai judgment (1994) made the proclamation justiciable and listed when its use is proper or improper.
concepts.rule: According to the chapter, President's Rule has been imposed on more than 125 occasions since 1950, first in Punjab in 1951, often arbitrarily. The Janata Government in 1977 and the Congress in 1980 each imposed it in nine states on the ground that the assemblies no longer represented the electorate. In 1992 it was imposed in three BJP-ruled states, which Bommai (1994) upheld because secularism is a basic feature; the Nagaland (1988), Karnataka (1989) and Meghalaya (1991) impositions were not upheld. The 38th Amendment made the President's satisfaction final and the 44th deleted that. Bommai held that the proclamation is justiciable, the Centre must prove relevant material, the court cannot examine its adequacy, it can restore the dismissed government, the assembly can only be suspended until Parliament approves, loss of majority is tested on the floor, and a new party at the Centre cannot dismiss other ministries. Proper and improper uses were listed from the Sarkaria Commission (pp.268-270).
concepts.example: A ministry that resigns after defeat in the assembly while no other party can form a government may justify President's Rule; a state ruling party's defeat in Lok Sabha elections may not.

questions.q: In Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the 1992 imposition of President's Rule in the BJP-ruled states on the ground that
questions.a: secularism is a 'basic feature' of the Constitution
o: secularism is a 'basic feature' of the Constitution
the Governors of those states had submitted reports of a breakdown of law and order
the assemblies no longer represented the wishes of the electorate after the Lok Sabha elections
no party had secured a majority in those assemblies after the general elections
questions.e: p.268: the Court upheld the validity of the 1992 proclamation on the ground that secularism is a 'basic feature'; p.269 adds that a state government pursuing anti-secular politics is liable to action under Article 356.
w: The ground was the state governments' failure to implement the ban on religious organisations sincerely, tested against secularism, not a Governor's report (p.268).
That was the reasoning of 1977 and 1980, which Bommai lists as improper (pp.268, 270).
The 1992 assemblies were not hung; hung assembly is a separate proper situation (p.270).

questions.q: When the Janata Government headed by Morarji Desai imposed President's Rule in nine Congress-ruled states in 1977, the ground given was that
questions.a: the assemblies in those states no longer represented the wishes of the electorate
o: the assemblies in those states no longer represented the wishes of the electorate
the state governments had refused to comply with directions of the Centre
the state governments were fomenting a violent revolt against the Constitution
none of the parties had a majority in the state assemblies
questions.e: p.268: the Janata Government imposed President's Rule in nine states on the ground that the assemblies no longer represented the wishes of the electorate; the Congress did the same in nine states in 1980.
w: The ground was the electorate's changed wishes after the Lok Sabha election, not a defiance of directions (p.268).
No internal subversion was alleged; the ground was political representation (p.268).
The assemblies had majorities; the ground was loss of representativeness (p.268).

questions.q: According to the Bommai propositions, when a court reviews the imposition of President's Rule, it
questions.a: cannot go into the correctness or adequacy of the material, but can see whether it is relevant to the action
o: cannot go into the correctness or adequacy of the material, but can see whether it is relevant to the action
can examine the correctness and adequacy of the material fully and substitute its own view
cannot examine the material at all, since the President's satisfaction is final and conclusive
can examine only whether the Governor's report was submitted before the proclamation
questions.e: p.269: the court cannot go into the correctness of the material or its adequacy but it can see whether it is relevant to the action; the action can be struck down if based on irrelevant or extraneous grounds or if malafide or perverse.
w: The court does not sit in judgment on correctness or adequacy (p.269).
The 38th Amendment's finality clause was deleted by the 44th Amendment (p.269).
The President can act even without a Governor's report, so review is not confined to that report (p.265).

questions.q: The 38th Amendment Act of 1975 made the satisfaction of the President in invoking Article 356 final and conclusive; the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 deleted that provision, implying that
questions.a: the satisfaction of the President is not beyond judicial review
o: the satisfaction of the President is not beyond judicial review
the satisfaction of the President can be reviewed only by Parliament
the President may now act only on a written recommendation of the Cabinet
the President may now act only on a report of the Governor of the state
questions.e: p.269: the provision was deleted by the 44th Amendment, implying that the satisfaction of the President is not beyond judicial review.
w: It is the courts, not Parliament, that can now review the satisfaction (p.269).
The written Cabinet recommendation is the 44th Amendment's safeguard for a National Emergency, not for Article 356 (p.260).
The President may act on the Governor's report or otherwise (p.265).

questions.q: Replying to critics of Article 356 in the Constituent Assembly, Dr B.R. Ambedkar hoped that the power conferred by it would
questions.a: remain a 'dead-letter' and be used only as a measure of last resort
o: remain a 'dead-letter' and be used only as a measure of last resort
be used liberally so that the Centre could intervene whenever a province was ill-governed
be exercised only after the Supreme Court had certified the failure of the constitutional machinery
be repealed once the first general elections had been held
questions.e: p.268: Ambedkar hoped the drastic power would remain a 'dead-letter' and would be used only as a measure of last resort; p.269 records H.V. Kamath's retort that 'Dr. Ambedkar is dead and the Articles are very much alive'.
w: He expected the power to be a last resort, not a liberal one (p.268).
No prior judicial certification was proposed; he hoped the President would take proper precautions (p.268-269).
He did not speak of repeal; he spoke of a dead-letter (p.268).

concepts.name: Financial Emergency (Article 360)
concepts.description: Grounds, judicial review, approval, duration and revocation, the financial directions to states and the Union, and the fact that none has been declared so far.
concepts.idea: A Financial Emergency under Article 360 gives the Centre full financial control over the states, needs only simple-majority approval within two months, has no maximum period, and has never been declared.
concepts.rule: Article 360 empowers the President to proclaim a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened. The 38th Amendment made the President's satisfaction final and conclusive, but the 44th Amendment deleted that, so it is open to judicial review. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months (with the usual 30-day rule if the Lok Sabha is dissolved), by a simple majority; once approved it continues until revoked, with no maximum period and no repeated approval, and the President may revoke it by a subsequent proclamation. The Centre may direct states to observe financial propriety, including reduction of salaries and reservation of money and financial bills for the President; the President may direct reduction of salaries of persons serving the Union, including judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. Ambedkar likened it to a US measure of 1933; none has been declared so far, though there was a financial crisis in 1991 (pp.270-272).
concepts.example: In a Financial Emergency the Centre may require a state to reserve its money bills for the President after the state legislature passes them.

concepts.name: Emergencies declared so far, the Shah Commission, and criticism and defence of the Emergency provisions
concepts.description: The 1962, 1971 and 1975 National Emergencies, the Shah Commission and the 44th Amendment, the Constituent Assembly debate for and against the Emergency provisions, and the Articles listed in Table 17.2.
concepts.idea: A National Emergency has been proclaimed three times (1962, 1971, 1975); the controversial 1975 one led to the Shah Commission and the 44th Amendment safeguards, echoing fears voiced in the Constituent Assembly.
concepts.rule: A National Emergency has been proclaimed three times. The first, in October 1962, followed Chinese aggression in the NEFA and was in force till January 1968, so no fresh proclamation was needed in 1965. The second, in December 1971, followed the attack by Pakistan; a third, in June 1975, was made while it was in operation, and both were revoked in March 1977. The first two were on external aggression; the third on internal disturbance, and proved the most controversial. After the Janata Party came to power in 1977 the Shah Commission was appointed, did not justify the declaration, and the 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards. In the Constituent Assembly, critics (Kamath, K.T. Shah, T.T. Krishnamachari, Kunzru) feared a dictatorship and loss of federal and financial autonomy, while Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and Mahabir Tyagi defended the provisions and Ambedkar accepted that they might be abused (pp.264-265, 272-273).
concepts.example: The Shah Commission, appointed after the 1977 elections, found no justification for the 1975 declaration, and the 44th Amendment followed in 1978.
